questions.question: What is the main purpose of HKDF-Extract (vs HKDF-Expand)?
options: Turn a potentially non-uniform secret into a pseudorandom key (PRK)
Encrypt a message with associated data (AEAD)
Generate an elliptic curve public key from a private scalar
Provide forward secrecy by deleting old chain keys
questions.explanation: HKDF-Extract uses HMAC with a salt to produce a pseudorandom key (PRK) even if the input secret isn't perfectly uniform.

questions.question: In an asynchronous messaging setting, what problem do “prekeys” primarily solve?
options: Let Alice establish a shared key with Bob while Bob is offline
Let Bob decrypt messages without any private keys stored
Hide message sizes from the network
Prevent spam by rate-limiting the server
questions.explanation: Prekeys are published ahead of time so an initiator can run a key agreement and send an initial encrypted message even if the recipient is offline.

questions.question: In X3DH without a one-time prekey, which DH values are KDFed to produce SK?
options: DH(IK_A, SPK_B) || DH(EK_A, IK_B) || DH(EK_A, SPK_B)
DH(IK_A, IK_B) || DH(SPK_A, SPK_B) || DH(EK_A, EK_B)
DH(IK_A, OPK_B) || DH(EK_A, OPK_B) || DH(EK_A, IK_B)
DH(SPK_A, IK_B) || DH(IK_A, IK_B) || DH(EK_A, IK_B)
questions.explanation: The basic X3DH run uses three DH computations (DH1..DH3) and optionally adds DH4 if an OPK is present.

questions.question: What is the role of AD (associated data) in the X3DH + Double Ratchet flow?
options: Bind identity information to AEAD so it is authenticated even if not encrypted
Provide randomness so X25519 outputs are never all-zero
Replace the need for a root key RK in the ratchet
Derive message keys MK directly without chain keys
questions.explanation: AD is authenticated by the AEAD (often concatenated with the header), helping bind the session to the intended identities.

questions.question: In the Double Ratchet, which action triggers a DH ratchet step?
options: Receiving a message whose header contains a new DH ratchet public key
Sending a message number N that is larger than 255
Any time HKDF-Expand is called with a different info string
Failing to decrypt a ciphertext due to a bad MAC
questions.explanation: A DH ratchet step occurs when a party receives a previously unseen DH ratchet public key from the other side.

questions.question: Why does the Double Ratchet derive a new message key for every message (via KDF_CK)?
options: So old message keys can be deleted to provide forward secrecy for past messages
So ciphertexts are shorter on the wire
So the server can verify integrity without client secrets
So the same message can be decrypted by multiple unrelated sessions
questions.explanation: A one-way chain creates single-use message keys; deleting old keys prevents recovering past keys after a compromise.

questions.question: How do skipped message keys (MKSKIPPED) help with out-of-order delivery?
options: The receiver can advance the receiving chain to N and cache keys for missing messages
The sender can reuse a message key until the receiver acknowledges it
The receiver can decrypt without tracking message numbers
The protocol becomes secure even without AEAD authentication
questions.explanation: If messages arrive out of order, the receiver derives and stores the intervening message keys so late messages can still be decrypted.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what can go wrong if Alice does not verify the signature on Bob’s signed prekey (SPK_B)?
options: A malicious server can substitute SPK_B and perform a man-in-the-middle on the initial session
Bob can never rotate prekeys without losing all messages
X25519 stops working and always outputs an all-zero shared secret
The Double Ratchet cannot handle out-of-order messages anymore
questions.explanation: If SPK_B isn't authenticated (signed by IK_B), the server can replace it and trick Alice into establishing a session with the attacker.
